title: Seventy sent (Luke 10:1–20)
hook: sent in pairs: say peace to this house first

segments.voice: Yesterday, he set his face toward Jerusalem. Your line was no looking back. Did you take the first step toward your hard thing? Day five hundred thirty-nine.

What's the first thing you say when you walk into someone's home? Hi. Sorry I'm late. Where should I put my shoes? Something smells amazing. Jesus is now on the road to Jerusalem, and he sends out a much bigger group than the twelve. In the King James words: "the Lord appointed other seventy also, and sent them two and two before his face into every city and place, whither he himself would come." Two by two. No one goes alone. Ahead of him, like people preparing the way. And before anything else, he tells them exactly what to say when they walk through a door.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU SAY AT THE DOOR?`

segments.voice: First, the honest warning: "The harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few." And: "behold, I send you forth as lambs among wolves." Not soldiers. Lambs. Then the packing list again, lighter than ever: no purse, no bag, no shoes, and don't stop to chat with everyone on the road. Then the doorway. "And into whatsoever house ye enter, first say, Peace be to this house." First. Before the message, before the meal, before anything. Behind the Greek word for peace stands the Hebrew greeting shalom, which reaches past the absence of fighting toward wholeness and well-being. Then a beautiful detail: "And if the son of peace be there, your peace shall rest upon it: if not, it shall turn to you again." Peace is like something you set down in a room. If someone there is open to it, it stays. If not, it comes back to you. You don't lose it by offering it. Stay in one house, he says. Eat what they put in front of you. Heal the sick. Say the kingdom of God has come near. And if a town won't welcome you, shake off the dust and move on. The seventy come back overjoyed: even the demons obey us in your name! And Jesus, gently, turns their joy in a better direction: "rejoice, because your names are written in heaven." Not in the power they had, he says, but in being known by name. Luke never names them. They aren't the twelve. They're a crowd of followers, sent ahead to the places he himself would come.
screen: `FIRST SAY, PEACE BE TO THIS HOUSE.`
then, large: `FIRST SAY, PEACE BE TO THIS HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say peace to a house. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a home you'll walk into soon. Your own, after work. A friend's. A parent's. A home where things are tense right now, or simply tired. Picture yourself at the door. Before you say anything about the traffic or what's for dinner, picture yourself bringing peace in with you, quietly, like setting down a gift. You don't have to say the words aloud. You can carry them in. Then let go of whether it's received. If it rests there, good. If not, it comes back to you. If you pray, you can say the line from Luke silently at the door. If you don't, simply bring calm in with you. The bell holds the time.
Seventy sent. Jesus sends out seventy, two by two, as lambs among wolves, and tells them to say first, at every door: peace be to this house.

Your line: peace be to this house. Bring it through the next door you open. And look back at the week: a hidden woman and a waking girl, five loaves, a daily cross, a shining face, a child, a road, and seventy at the door. Day five hundred thirty-nine, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: In the Book of Common Prayer, the order for the visitation of the sick opens with "Peace be to this house," and some Christians use the same words when blessing a home.

fork.setup: you're one of the seventy, at the door of a stranger's house. what do you say first?
fork.reveal: peace comes first. if a son of peace is there, it rests on the house; if not, it returns to you.

original.note: Greek: peace. in Jesus' world the greeting was shalom: wholeness and well-being.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mission trip.
what it means: seventy ordinary followers sent ahead in pairs, told to offer peace first at every door and let it rest or return.
what a scholar hears: "before his face" is the phrase Luke used a chapter earlier for the messengers sent ahead into Samaria (9:52): the seventy go to prepare his road.

Use of 'Peace be to this house' in Catholic and Anglican rites (visitation of the sick in the Book of Common Prayer; house blessings) stated generally in howItsDone. Confirm.
